# Part 1 · Setup and descriptive statistics

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# Read in the data file
grayling_df <- read_csv("data/gray_I3_I8.csv")

i3_df <- grayling_df %>% filter(lake == "I3")

head(grayling_df)
```

**▶ Run this — summary statistics by lake:**

``` r
grayling_summary <- grayling_df %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_length = mean(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_length = sd(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_length = sd_length / sqrt(sum(!is.na(length_mm))),
    count = sum(!is.na(length_mm)),
    .groups = "drop")

grayling_summary
```

# Part 2 · The standard normal distribution and Z-scores

**Z score = (length − mean) / standard deviation**

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of fish lengths
mean_length <- mean(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_length <- sd(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate Z-scores for fish lengths
i3_df <- i3_df %>%
  mutate(z_score = (length_mm - mean_length) / sd_length)

# View the first few rows with Z-scores
head(i3_df)
```

**▶ Run this — plot the Z-scores:**

``` r
z_fish_plot <- i3_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = z_score)) +
  geom_histogram()

z_fish_plot
```

Remember, in a true normal distribution, approximately:

-   68% of data within ±1σ of the mean
-   **95% of data within ±2σ of the mean — really 1.96σ**
-   99.7% of data within ±3σ of the mean

**▶ Run this — check the 68% rule against our own data:**

``` r
# What proportion of fish are within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
within_1sd <- sum(abs(i3_df$z_score) <= 1, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(!is.na(i3_df$z_score))
cat("Proportion within 1 SD:", round(within_1sd * 100, 1), "%\n")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Is the proportion you calculated close to 68%? If not, what might explain the difference (think about sample size and how closely I3 follows a true normal distribution)? `________________________`

# Part 3 · Using R for Z-score probabilities

R gives us `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, and `dnorm()` so we never have to integrate area under the curve by hand.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# For standard normal distribution (mean=0, sd=1):
# pnorm(z)  gives cumulative probability (area to the left)
# qnorm(p)  gives z-value for a given probability
# dnorm(z)  gives probability density

z_value <- 1.22
prob_left <- pnorm(z_value)          # area to the left of z
prob_right <- 1 - pnorm(z_value)     # area to the right of z
prob_between <- pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2) # area between two z-values

# To find z-value for a given probability:
z_for_95_percent <- qnorm(0.888)

print(prob_left)
print(prob_right)
print(prob_between)
print(z_for_95_percent)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** By hand (or with `pnorm()`), for a fish that is 300 mm long: `z = (300 - 265.61)/28.3 = 1.215194`. What proportion of fish are expected to be **longer** than 300 mm? `________________________`

**▶ Run this — the cutoff for an "unlikely" catch:**

``` r
# What fish length corresponds to the top 5% (unlikely)?
top_5_percent_z <- qnorm(0.95)  # z-score for 95th percentile
unlikely_length <- mean_length + (top_5_percent_z * sd_length)

cat("Only 5% of fish are longer than:", round(unlikely_length, 1), "mm\n")
cat("This corresponds to z-score:", round(top_5_percent_z, 3), "\n")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** In one sentence, explain what `unlikely_length` means in plain, non-statistical language — as if you were telling another angler. `________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** `pnorm()`/`qnorm()` give you the area under the *theoretical* standard normal curve. You can also estimate probability directly from your *own* data's empirical density curve with R's `density()` function — try `dens <- density(i3_df$length_mm)` and see if you can find the proportion of the area between 320 and 350 mm. Ask your instructor if you'd like the walk-through code for this.
:::

# Part 4 · Standard error, confidence intervals, and the t-distribution

When the population standard deviation is unknown and *n* is small (\< \~30), we use the **Student's t-distribution** instead of the standard normal (z) distribution:

$$\text{CI} = \bar{y} \pm t \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

**▶ Run this — draw a small sample and compare a z-based CI to a t-based CI:**

``` r
small_sample <- grayling_df %>% filter(lake == "I3") %>% slice_sample(n = 10)
sample_mean <- mean(small_sample$length_mm)
sample_sd <- sd(small_sample$length_mm)
sample_n <- nrow(small_sample)
sample_se <- sample_sd / sqrt(sample_n)

z_ci_lower <- sample_mean - 1.96 * sample_se
z_ci_upper <- sample_mean + 1.96 * sample_se

t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = sample_n - 1)
t_ci_lower <- sample_mean - t_crit * sample_se
t_ci_upper <- sample_mean + t_crit * sample_se

cat("Mean:", round(sample_mean, 1), "mm\n")
cat("Standard deviation:", round(sample_sd, 2), "mm\n")
cat("Standard error:", round(sample_se, 2), "mm\n")
cat("95% CI using z:", round(z_ci_lower, 1), "to", round(z_ci_upper, 1), "mm\n")
cat("95% CI using t:", round(t_ci_lower, 1), "to", round(t_ci_upper, 1), "mm\n")
cat("t critical value:", round(t_crit, 3), "vs z critical value: 1.96\n")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which interval is wider — the z-based or the t-based CI? Why does using the t-distribution make sense here instead of z? `________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Re-run the `slice_sample(n = 10)` line a few times (each run draws a different random sample). Does the t-based CI change more, less, or about the same as the z-based CI each time?
:::

# Part 5 · One-sample t-test

Does the mean fish length in Lake I3 differ from 260 mm?

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# get only lake I3
i3_df <- grayling_df %>% filter(lake == "I3")

# what is the mean
i3_mean <- mean(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Mean:", round(i3_mean, 1), "mm\n")

# Perform a one-sample t-test
t_test_result <- t.test(i3_df$length_mm, mu = 260)

# View the test results
t_test_result
```

# Part 6 · Two-sample t-test — comparing lakes

**Research question:** Are fish in Lake I8 longer than fish in Lake I3?

✏️ **Your turn — before running any code:** Write the null and alternative hypotheses for this question.

```
H0: ________________________
Ha: ________________________
```

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Perform an independent t-test
t_test_result <- t.test(length_mm ~ lake, data = grayling_df,
                       alternative = "less")  # H0: mu_I3 >= mu_I8, H1: mu_I3 < mu_I8

# Display the results
t_test_result
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Based on this t-test, what can we conclude about the difference in fish length between the two lakes? `________________________`

# Part 7 · P-values, Type I/II errors, and power

A **p-value** is the probability of observing the sample result (or something more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true. Remember:

-   p-value is NOT the probability that H₀ is true
-   p-value is NOT the probability that results occurred by chance
-   statistical significance ≠ practical significance

✏️ **Your turn:** For each scenario below, identify whether a Type I or Type II error might have occurred.

1.  A researcher concludes that a new fishing regulation increased grayling size, when in fact it had no effect. `________________________`
2.  A study fails to detect a real decline in grayling population due to warming water, concluding there was no effect. `________________________`

**▶ Run this — calculate the power of our t-test to detect a 30 mm difference in length between lakes:**

``` r
# First determine parameters
lake_I3 <- grayling_df %>% filter(lake == "I3")
lake_I8 <- grayling_df %>% filter(lake == "I8")

n1 <- nrow(lake_I3)
n2 <- nrow(lake_I8)
sd_pooled <- sqrt((var(lake_I3$length_mm) * (n1 - 1) +
                  var(lake_I8$length_mm) * (n2 - 1)) /
                  (n1 + n2 - 2))

# Calculate power
effect_size <- 30 / sd_pooled  # Cohen's d
df <- n1 + n2 - 2
alpha <- 0.05
power <- power.t.test(n = min(n1, n2),
                     delta = effect_size,
                     sd = 1,  # Using standardized effect size
                     sig.level = alpha,
                     type = "two.sample",
                     alternative = "two.sided")

power
```

✏️ **Your turn:** What does the `power` value tell you about our ability to detect a real 30 mm difference between lakes with our current sample size? Would a bigger sample size increase or decrease power? `________________________`

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Spelling? Did you forget `na.rm = TRUE`?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
